title: Bar Model Word Problems
intro: A bar model organizes the quantities in a story. The top bar names the whole, and the two lower parts fit together to make it. Find which quantity is missing, fill its box, and connect the diagram to an equation.
html:
A diagram should explain the relationship

Maya has 9 library books and receives 5 more. She begins drawing fourteen tiny books, then loses count. A bar model lets her keep the relationship visible without drawing every object. Nine and five are the two parts; the new total is the whole.

Total?
95

9 + 5 = 14

The whole is fourteen because both parts belong to it.

Move the unknown, and the calculation changes

Now the class has 14 books after receiving 5. We know the whole and the new books, but not the starting collection. Put fourteen in the whole bar, five in one part, and a question mark in the other.

Total14
?5

14 − 5 = 9

Nine books were there before the new books arrived.

Both diagrams describe a whole made of two parts. The position of the blank shows which quantity needs to be found. The bars in these worksheets organize numbers; they are not rulers. Do not measure the printed lengths to calculate an answer.

Use a part-whole model for an amount taken away

If there were 17 cookies and 6 remain after some were used, the starting seventeen is the whole. The used amount and the remaining six are the parts. Subtract the known remaining part from the whole: 17 − 6 = 11. Then check that 11 + 6 rebuilds seventeen.

If the child adds every visible number: point to the whole bar and the two parts below it. The whole already includes both parts. Adding the whole again would count the same collection twice.

Read the model back into the story

Ask the child to name each region before writing the equation. In a receiving story, a part might mean the books there before. In a taking-away story, that same position might represent cookies used. The shape alone does not supply the object or the event; the sentence does.

These four questions include an unknown total, an unknown starting amount, and an unknown amount used, with numbers within twenty. They use part-whole bars, not comparison bars or multiplication models. The answer key fills the same blank and shows one suitable equation.

Use the relationship with larger numbers

When the child can explain what the whole and both parts mean, try missing part word problems within 100. That guide shows a worked bar example, and its printable leaves space for the child to draw or show a method. It does not supply a preprinted bar for every question.

Keep this four-question bar-model set when the child still needs the diagram provided. Its numbers remain within twenty. In either set, read the labels to identify quantities: a diagram can organize the relationship without giving each part a length proportional to its value.
